geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better reconstructs the spherical wedge geometry because it correctly maps the textbook vertical z-axis to Three.js' vertical axis, builds the six bounding surfaces of the spherical shell wedge, and places the θ and φ arcs in the appropriate coordinate planes. Figure 2 also constructs plausible spherical-coordinate patches, but it uses z as the mathematical vertical axis while the camera/view setup treats y as vertical, so the labeled y-axis appears as the vertical axis and the z-axis is a receding horizontal axis, making the initial 3D geometry/viewpoint substantially less faithful to the standard textbook figure.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2's sliders consistently update the underlying state, redraw the wedge and construction surfaces, keep the displayed numeric values synchronized, and enforce valid ordering at extremes, whereas Figure 1's sliders redraw the wedge but use much more restrictive non-overlapping ranges, provide no live value feedback, and its polar-angle controls do not update the transparent construction sector as completely. Figure 2 is not perfect because its rebuilds leave stale registered interactive objects and it changes paired slider values to maintain constraints, but its requested slider interactions are still more complete and informative than Figure 1's.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is much more recognizable as the textbook spherical-coordinate volume element: it preserves the translucent spherical sector, black coordinate axes, radius/angle annotations, and a green highlighted curved wedge similar to the original. Figure 2 reduces the scene to a simple orange wedge with a different axis orientation and lacks the large translucent shell, layered colored patch, and rho bracket construction, so it reads much less like the reference at a glance.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has larger, more readable labels for the axes and angular bounds, whereas Figure 1’s diagram labels are extremely small and many are barely legible at the shown size. Figure 1 does include more of the original-style distance annotations such as the vertical ρ labels, but their tiny size and weak visibility make them less useful; Figure 2’s labels are clearer overall, though it misplaces/changes some annotation geometry relative to the reference and has some crowding near the wedge.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 more truthfully represents the wedge as the solid bounded by the six stated coordinate surfaces: two spherical shells ρ=ρ₁,ρ₂, two θ half-planes, and two φ cones measured from the z-axis, and its tooltip states those six surfaces explicitly (L00007-L00012, L00015). Figure 1 also builds the main six surfaces, but it is less conceptually clean: its construction shell adds an equatorial φ=π/2 surface rather than showing the two polar cone bounds as the transparent sector surfaces, and its color assignment is more inconsistent with the source distinction of green spheres, yellow half-planes, and pink cones (L00009-L00011).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 2 has the slight overall edge because it more clearly labels the diagram, provides more complete and informative slider behavior, and more explicitly represents the intended six bounding coordinate surfaces, whereas Figure 1’s controls and labels are less usable and its conceptual construction is less clean. However, Figure 1 is stronger visually and geometrically: it more closely resembles the textbook rendering and preserves the standard vertical z-axis viewpoint better than Figure 2, whose axis orientation is less faithful. The decision is therefore close, but Figure 2’s advantages across interactivity, labels, and conceptual correctness narrowly outweigh Figure 1’s stronger visual faithfulness.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better preserves the periodic-table topology, group/period placement, common-ion labels, f-block separation, red placeholder outline with arrow, and especially the intended charge-category structure by treating transition and f-block elements as variable rather than assigning them fixed charges. Figure 2 has the same basic table layout, but it is more schematic and less faithful in the charge-color mode, incorrectly coloring transition metals and f-block cells as typical fixed positive charges and using a more generic/less exact structural encoding of several regions.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 implements the requested controls much more correctly: clicking cells creates a visible selection highlight and updates an information panel/popup with charge labels, electron-configuration information when available, and the relevant group-rule explanation; its 1–18 slider highlights the selected column and reports the typical group behavior; and its color-scheme toggle actually redraws all cells using a charge/category scheme. Figure 2’s controls are materially weaker: cell clicks only show a generic popup and do not highlight the cell or provide electron configurations, many cells only report a generic typical charge, the group slider includes an extra 0/All state and does not show the typical ion for the selected group, and its charge-coloring handler computes misleading fixed charges for transition metals rather than variable behavior.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful: it preserves the reference’s blue group numbers, purple period numbering, pastel category colors, red outlined f-block insertion area, red arrow, and overall periodic-table composition more closely. Figure 2 has the same general layout but looks less like the original because the labels are mostly black, the table is more compressed, the red f-block annotation is reduced and awkward, and the asterisks appear inside the main table rather than matching the reference’s placement.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 has more legible and correctly styled main table labels, with the blue group numbers and ionic labels generally clearer and better placed than in Figure 2. Figure 2 does include the vertical Period label that Figure 1 omits, but many of its labels are very small, less faithful in color/weight, and it incorrectly adds '*' and '**' inside the group-3 placeholder cells, creating extra non-original annotations and clutter.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately represents the stated common ion-charge table: its labels closely match the specified ions, leaves noble gases without charge labels, and treats transition metals as variable rather than predictable by group position (L00010, L00014, L00019). Figure 2 includes the main labels, but its tooltip and charge-color logic assigns a single “typical charge” of +2 to all transition metals and to several unlabeled p-block elements, which contradicts the required point that transition-metal charges are variable and not reliably predicted by location (L00010, L00019); its narration also overstates that main-group positions dictate exact charges rather than tendencies/guides (L00010, L00019).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is clearly stronger overall: it more faithfully matches the reference styling and layout, preserves the intended periodic-table topology and f-block annotation, and implements the interactions more completely with cell highlighting, informative panels, group behavior, and a functioning charge/category color mode. Figure 2 shares the broad table structure but is weaker visually and conceptually, with less faithful labels and annotations, generic or incomplete interactivity, and misleading fixed-charge treatment of transition metals and f-block elements where variable charges are intended.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better matches the likely textbook geometry: a front-on balance apparatus with the sample tube suspended in the electromagnet gap, a right-side pan, a vertical support, leader labels, and field-line structure in the correct spatial relationship. Figure 2 uses real 3D primitives but its proportions are exaggerated, the camera is set almost along the beam axis so the balance geometry is viewed from an inappropriate depth perspective, and the apparatus layout becomes less faithful to the original front-view schematic.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1's controls correctly recompute the beam tilt, tube displacement, field-line intensity, and susceptibility readout for both paramagnetic and diamagnetic cases, and its energize animation visibly ramps the field from zero while drawing or repelling the tube in the correct direction. Figure 2's sample and field controls do change the beam direction and field opacity, but it provides no susceptibility sign/value readout at all, its energize button only ramps to maximum and can do nothing if already there, and the weighing animation is much less specifically tied to the tube being drawn into or repelled from the magnet gap.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is much more recognizable as the textbook figure because it includes the balance beam with hanging sample, opposing electromagnets, purple magnetic field lines, labels, and a weight pan on the right, even though its colors and proportions are crude. Figure 2 shows a simplified dark balance-like object but largely loses the key visual structure of the original: the sample-in-field setup, labeled electromagnets, magnetic field lines, and broad left-right composition are not clearly represented.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 includes the key textbook annotations "Sample," "Magnetic field," and "Electromagnets" in readable text near the relevant parts, whereas Figure 2 lacks the original diagram labels entirely and only shows unrelated UI controls. Figure 1 does add extra interface text and an invented "x = +1.50" label, and its placement is not perfect, but it still matches the required annotations far better than Figure 2.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 more truthfully preserves the core physical relationships: the sample tube is suspended in the gap between electromagnets opposite a pan of weights, and paramagnetic versus diamagnetic choices tip the sample side downward versus upward consistently with apparent heavier/lighter behavior (L00010, L00014, L00016, L00019). Figure 1 depicts the apparatus and force directions well, but it adds a prominent χ readout computed from field strength and sample sign, which falsely suggests magnetic susceptibility itself varies with the applied field; the brief instead frames the measured change in apparent mass as the experimental observable used to infer unpaired electrons (L00010, L00019).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the clear overall winner because it much more faithfully presents the intended balance apparatus: the hanging sample in the electromagnet gap, right-side pan, magnetic field lines, and key labels are recognizable, while Figure 2 loses many of these schematic elements and has an awkward perspective and incomplete labeling. Figure 1 also implements the intended interactions more completely, including field ramping, tube displacement, beam tilt, and susceptibility-related feedback; Figure 2 has some correct paramagnetic/diamagnetic behavior but lacks the readout and its energize/weighing behavior is less tied to the apparatus. Although Figure 1's susceptibility readout may imply a questionable dependence on field strength, that conceptual flaw is outweighed by Figure 2's broader visual, geometric, labeling, and interaction shortcomings.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 is geometrically stronger because it builds the apparatus from actual 3D primitives—cylindrical transparent beaker and liquid, volumetric electrodes, curved tube wires, spherical particles, and a bulb assembly with real depth—so the spatial relationships between plug, electrodes, solution, and bulb are more coherent. Figure 2 is flatter and less accurate geometrically: the beaker and liquid are simplified box slabs, the initial camera is essentially head-on with little depth, and the ions/molecules are 2D canvas sprites rather than true 3D particle geometry, which makes the reconstruction less faithful as a 3D figure.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1’s solution selector, concentration slider, and motion checkbox consistently rebuild the particle population and bulb brightness so the drawn ions and glow agree across the allowed states, and its ions actually migrate toward the appropriate electrodes before wrapping. Figure 2’s controls mostly work, but at low weak-electrolyte concentrations it can show nonzero bulb brightness with no ions drawn, ethanol at zero concentration still shows neutral molecules, and its migrating ions wrap near the center rather than reaching the plates, so the advertised effects are less correct at extremes.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more recognizable as the textbook conductivity setup because it clearly shows a glowing bulb for KCl, labeled positive and negative electrodes, charged ions in solution, and the KCl/high conductivity caption. Figure 1 has the general plug-wire-beaker arrangement, but its electrodes are barely represented, the bulb is less recognizable, the particle depiction is less faithful to the ethanol/no-conductivity panel, and the key visual cues from the original are weaker.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has the key solution and conductivity labels ('KCl' and 'High conductivity') clearly readable beneath the apparatus and places the electrode +/− signs legibly, whereas Figure 1’s corresponding 'ethanol / No conductivity' label is tiny, placed inside the beaker, and difficult to read at inline size. Both figures include extra interface text not present in the textbook figure and neither shows all three original captions simultaneously, but Figure 2’s main scientific labels are much closer in readability and placement to the reference.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately teaches the key distinctions: ethanol has only neutral clusters and a dark bulb, KCl has many +/− ions migrating to opposite electrodes, and acetic acid has many undissociated molecules with only a few ions and a dim bulb, matching the nonelectrolyte/strong/weak electrolyte concepts and the stated ion-migration directions (L00012, L00016). Figure 2 gets the general directions and conductivity-brightness relationship mostly right, but its weak-electrolyte acetic acid state visually overrepresents dissociation by showing roughly comparable or even more ions than neutral molecule clusters, which weakens the intended “only a few labeled ions alongside undissociated molecule clusters” idea (L00016).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because its 3D apparatus, ion/electrode geometry, concentration behavior, and conceptual distinctions among ethanol, KCl, and acetic acid are more accurate than Figure 2’s flatter construction, sprite-like particles, center-wrapping ion motion, and over-dissociated weak-electrolyte depiction. Figure 2 is visually more readable in the rendered screenshot, with clearer KCl/high-conductivity and electrode labels, but those labeling advantages do not outweigh Figure 1’s better underlying scientific behavior and spatial reconstruction.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better preserves the textbook-style 2D structure: a broad green enzyme with a clearly complementary active-site cavity, two distinct substrate pieces with matching protrusions, leader lines from the substrate label, docking arrows, and labels matching the original concepts such as “Active site is proper shape” and “Substrate complex formed.” Figure 2 conveys the same idea but its substrates are more generic blob shapes with less precise complementarity to the active site, adds extra elements such as a dashed original-site outline and panel title, and its bound layout/label placement is less faithful to the likely original diagram structure.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1's model toggle and dock button consistently update the drawing, button label, substrate positions, and enzyme shape, including a real animated conformational change for induced fit and no enzyme reshaping for lock-and-key. Figure 2's controls mostly redraw correctly, but its Dock substrate button only cycles through idle/docking/bound in separate clicks with a static misleading label and no actual continuous docking animation, so the advertised interaction is less correctly implemented.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more visually faithful because its composition, two separate active-site pockets, substrate placement, arrows, and labels more closely resemble the lock-and-key portion of the reference. Figure 2 preserves the general idea but simplifies the substrates into generic semicircles and collapses the enzyme binding area into a central jagged notch, making it look less like the original geometry.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 includes the important panel caption “(a) Lock-and-key model,” which Figure 1 omits, and its label set more closely matches the reference for this state. Figure 1 has somewhat cleaner and larger placement for the enzyme label, but it is missing the original caption and therefore is less complete; Figure 2’s enzyme label is cramped against the enzyme outline, but overall its labels and annotations are more faithful.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately conveys the central distinction: lock-and-key has a pre-formed, complementary active site that remains unchanged on binding, while induced fit begins less exactly matched and changes shape to make the complex (L00007, L00010, L00017). Figure 2 also shows the broad distinction, but its narration says compatibility may be “created by binding,” which overstates induced fit and can imply the enzyme is too malleable or nonspecific, contrary to the requirement that both models preserve substrate specificity and only structurally compatible substrates bind (L00010, L00017); its lock-and-key substrate/cavity shapes are also less explicitly complementary than Figure 1’s rounded/pointed matching depressions and projections (L00014).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because it more faithfully preserves the textbook-style enzyme/substrate geometry, with distinct complementary substrate pieces, clear active-site pockets, docking arrows, and a lock-and-key/induced-fit distinction that is conceptually accurate. Compared with Figure 1, Figure 2 has a useful panel caption and somewhat more complete labeling, but its generic substrate shapes, less precise active-site complementarity, weaker docking interaction, and potentially misleading induced-fit narration make it less successful overall.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better reconstructs the likely textbook structure because it preserves the three-panel layout with labels a), b), c), transformation arrows/captions between panels, the original 6-node/8-edge graph, the intermediate overlay of edge-nodes, and the final 8-node edge graph with the correct shared-endpoint connections. Figure 2 has the same underlying graph topology and computes the correct edge-graph adjacency, but it collapses the textbook sequence into a single overlaid phased view rather than separate panels, omits the side-by-side comparative layout and inter-panel arrows, and therefore is structurally less faithful despite having correct node/edge counts.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2’s step buttons and phase radios consistently drive the advertised construction states, and clicking an edge/node in the connected or final phases correctly highlights the corresponding edge-node and its generated line-graph connections. Figure 1 has working step buttons and edge highlighting in the final state, but its “View: Edge graph” toggle only changes panel opacity and can leave the edge-graph panel empty if used before the construction reaches that step; likewise, edge clicks in early steps highlight hidden line-graph nodes/connections, so the interaction often fails to show what it claims.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more recognizable as the full textbook figure because it preserves the three-panel left-to-right construction, orange and teal node scheme, panel labels, arrows, and captions. Figure 2 renders the original graph panel much more cleanly and at a more faithful scale, but in this screenshot it only shows the first panel, so it is less immediately identifiable as the complete transformation figure; Figure 1 is smaller and less accurate in details, especially with the later panels looking cramped/faded, but its overall composition matches the reference better.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 includes the original figure's main panel labels and annotations such as a), b), c), 'Original graph,' 'Edge graph,' edge-node labels, and the arrow captions, even though many are very small and hard to read at inline size. Figure 2 has readable node labels and UI text, but it only shows the first-stage graph and omits most of the textbook figure's required labels and annotations, including the b/c panels, edge-node labels, titles, and transformation captions.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately instantiates the line-graph construction as specified: it shows an original undirected graph, places one teal node at each original edge, and computes/draws edges between new nodes exactly when the corresponding original edges share an endpoint, with a distinct final edge-graph panel labeled by endpoint pairs (L00007). Figure 2 uses the same correct edge-to-node and shared-endpoint rule, but it collapses the requested three labeled sub-panels into a single phased overlay, so the original, intermediate, and final graphs are not simultaneously distinguished as panels a, b, and c, making the construction less faithful to the stated presentation even though the underlying rule is mostly correct (L00007).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the stronger overall reconstruction because it preserves the textbook’s three-panel sequence, panel labels, transformation arrows/captions, original graph, intermediate edge-node overlay, and final line graph with the correct shared-endpoint adjacencies. Figure 2 has cleaner and more reliable interactive controls, and its underlying line-graph rule is correct, but relative to Figure 1 it collapses the construction into a single phased view and omits much of the required labeled, side-by-side presentation.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 better matches the BRDF-style 3D geometry: it uses a broad rectangular surface with border, a single interaction point, a vertical normal, tangent directions, a correctly placed incoming ray, and a moderate hemispherical set of outgoing reflection arrows with a distinct specular direction. Figure 2 is more generic and less faithful geometrically: its square plane, orthogonal p/q frame with extra right-angle brackets, very dense 80-ray hemisphere, and different camera/view proportions make the figure look less like the intended textbook diagram and distort the element count and spatial emphasis.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 better satisfies the intended interactions because the incoming ray itself is draggable over the upper hemisphere and each drag recomputes the outgoing BRDF arrow lengths, opacity, specular direction, tooltip radiance values, and the incident-ray label in real time; its roughness slider and demo buttons also consistently update the displayed value and lobe. Figure 2's sliders and material buttons do redraw the lobe and demos mostly work, but it does not allow dragging the incoming ray directly, constrains the incident direction to a narrower angular range, and its 'Light Elevation' control is effectively a polar angle from the normal rather than a true elevation, making the advertised interaction less correct.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 is more recognizable as the reference because it preserves the green surface, central point, labeled p/q/n directions, a diagonal yellow-orange incident ray, and surrounding reflected/scattered green arrows. Figure 2 has the green plane and axes but changes the main incident/outgoing geometry into mostly vertical rays and omits much of the reference composition, making it read less like the original textbook diagram.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 has more of the original labeling content present and readable, including a clear formula label in the side panel and visible p, n, q labels, whereas Figure 2's original-relevant labels are extremely small, cluttered near the center, and the incident/outgoing light labels are not readable or properly placed. Figure 2 also includes many invented UI labels that do not correspond to the textbook figure, while Figure 1's extra UI text is less harmful because it at least includes the key formula clearly.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more accurately teaches the core BRDF idea by displaying the stated functional dependence ℓ_out = F(ℓ_in, n, λ, p, q) and by showing many outgoing directions from one incident ray, matching the dependence on incoming and outgoing ray directions and wavelength (L00011-L00017, L00033-L00034). Figure 2 also shows hemispherical scattering, but its diffuse mode makes outgoing ray length vary strongly with outgoing angle and still highlights a mirror-like peak, which can mislead students about diffuse/Lambertian behavior where the simplified model is independent of q and depends on n·p instead (L00024-L00030). Both figures are imperfect because they label p and q as surface tangent-frame arrows rather than clearly as the incident and outgoing ray directions defined in the textbook context (L00009-L00015), but Figure 1’s equation and directional BRDF emphasis are closer to the intended concept than Figure 2’s misleading diffuse/specular assertions.

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the clear overall winner: it more closely preserves the intended BRDF geometry and rendered composition, with a green surface, central interaction point, p/q/n labels, a diagonal incident ray, and a moderate set of outgoing scattering arrows, while Figure 2 looks more generic and distorts the emphasis with a dense vertical-looking hemisphere and cluttered central labels. Figure 1 also implements the intended interaction more completely by allowing the incoming ray itself to be dragged and updating the lobe, specular direction, opacity, tooltip values, and labels in real time, whereas Figure 2 relies on sliders, constrains the incident direction, and mislabels its light-elevation behavior. Conceptually and textually, Figure 1 better communicates the BRDF dependence with a clear formula and directional scattering, while Figure 2’s diffuse/specular behavior and extra UI labels are more misleading relative to the textbook figure.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 is geometrically more accurate because it constructs both camera centers, image planes, true rays to the 3D point, projected image points, and clipped epipolar lines on both planes from the epipolar-plane normal. Figure 2 has the basic two-plane/two-ray setup, but it does not actually draw the epipolar line segments despite labeling ℓ1 and ℓ2, uses mostly static decorative arrows, lets p' leave the plane without meaningful clipping, and its translation update moves the world point with the target camera rather than preserving the intended spatial relationship.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 1 has the more correct live interaction model: changing depth, translation, or rotation triggers a single update that recomputes the 3D point, both rays, the reference projection p', epipolar lines, moving arrows, labels, and displayed slider values consistently. Figure 2 does update P, p, p', and the rays, but several advertised visual elements such as the R,T arrow and P'=MP loop are static and no longer track the geometry, its step narration for translation claims P is fixed even though the code moves P with the target camera, and it lacks value feedback; overall its controls work but less completely and coherently than Figure 1.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 2 is more visually faithful because it preserves the main left-target/right-reference composition, the elevated 3D point P, dashed projection rays, red projected points, black camera centers, and the grey rotation/translation arcs in roughly the same spatial relationship as the original. Figure 1 contains some of the same ingredients, but its overall layout is much less recognizable: P is displaced to the far left rather than above the reference frame, the dashed rays run almost horizontally, the frame arrangement and arrow structure do not match the original composition as well, and the labels/arcs are harder to associate with the textbook figure.

labels.rationale: Figure 2 has most of the required labels from the original (P=zK^-1p, P'=MP, p'=KP, p, P, p', l1/l2, Target frame, Reference frame, R,T) and they are generally larger and more readable. Figure 1 includes some corresponding labels, but the whole diagram is much smaller, many labels are nearly unreadable or cramped, and important annotations are harder to identify; its side UI text also visually competes with the diagram.

concept.rationale: Figure 1 more truthfully represents the two-view reconstruction pipeline: p is back-projected along the target ray to P with depth z, the reference camera is related by R,T, and p' is obtained by projecting the same 3D point onto the reference image plane, matching the brief’s P = zK⁻¹p, rigid motion, and p' = KP relationships (L00010). Figure 2 includes the same formula labels, but its interactive narration and geometry are less conceptually accurate: when translation changes it claims P is fixed while the code recomputes P from the moving target camera, and its R,T and P'=MP arrows are largely static rather than tied to the actual transformed point/frame relationship, which can mislead students about the two-frame constraint between corresponding points (L00007-L00010).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is stronger overall because its source-driven geometry and interaction model consistently recompute the camera centers, rays, projections, epipolar lines, labels, and slider-dependent relationships, whereas Figure 2 leaves important elements such as epipolar line segments, R,T arrows, and transformation annotations static or inconsistent with the updated scene. Figure 2 is visually closer to the reference screenshot and has larger, more readable labels, but those presentation advantages are outweighed by Figure 1’s more accurate two-view reconstruction concept and more coherent behavior under depth, translation, and rotation changes.

geometry.rationale: Figure 1 more closely reconstructs the likely textbook geometry: it uses an oblique front-on projection matching the drawn axes, places a vertical projection plane with local x/y axes, shows the two-step block, parallel projection lines, and simple projected colored faces in roughly the expected spatial relationship. Figure 2 models a more general interactive projection demo with a different isometric camera, a deeper extruded staircase, many extra rays and projected stepped polygons, plus optional perspective/pinhole/depth-guide machinery; even if pedagogically useful, these additions and altered proportions/viewpoint make it less faithful to the original figure geometry.

interactivity.rationale: Figure 2 implements the requested interactions much more completely and correctly: its projection blend slider recomputes rays, projected shapes, pinhole visibility, and depth-guide projections; the guide toggle updates equal-length bars at different depths; and dragging the object yaws the staircase while recomputing the orthographic/perspective projection. Figure 1 only provides a Z-position slider that moves the object and rays while leaving the orthographic image fixed, which is a valid limited depth-independence demonstration, but it omits the orthographic-to-perspective blend, depth-guide toggle, and object-rotation/projection-update interaction entirely. Figure 2 has minor implementation blemishes such as some projected outline line objects being offset in z, but its controls substantially match the advertised effects, whereas Figure 1 covers only a small subset.

faithfulness.rationale: Figure 1 more closely matches the reference at a glance: it keeps the projection plane on the left, the colored 3D block on the right, dashed horizontal projection guides between them, and the projected colored shape on the plane. Figure 2 has the same general colors and a projection plane, but its camera angle and layout reverse/rotate the composition, the object sits much closer to or in front of the plane, and the characteristic long dashed correspondence lines and rightward separated solid from the textbook figure are largely missing in the shown view.

labels.rationale: Figure 1 better matches the original labeling set with X, Y, Z, lowercase x/y, and Projection plane present with relatively little added text; its labels are small but mostly readable and less cluttered. Figure 2 has readable axis labels, but the Projection plane label overlaps the artwork more, and the large right-side UI/instruction text introduces many labels not present in the original, making the screenshot more cluttered and less faithful.

concept.rationale: Figure 2 more truthfully teaches orthographic projection: it uses a projection plane perpendicular to the labeled Z axis and maps points as (X,Y,Z) to (X,Y,plane), with dashed rays parallel to Z at the orthographic setting, matching x=X and y=Y and the requirement for parallel rays orthogonal to the plane (L00007, L00010). It also correctly demonstrates distance independence with equal-depth guides and a true perspective contrast at the endpoint, whereas Figure 1 shows the same basic idea but only connects a subset of corners, uses a more indirect relabeling of axes, and its projected colored layout is less complete and less clearly tied to all corners/faces of the staircase solid (L00010).

aggregator.explanation: Figure 1 is the stronger overall reconstruction because it more closely matches the reference geometry and rendered appearance: the projection plane, separated block, dashed correspondence lines, projected colored faces, and original-style labels are arranged much more like the textbook figure than in Figure 2. Figure 2 is notably better as an interactive and conceptual projection demo, with richer controls and a more complete orthographic/perspective treatment, but it departs more from the target figure through its altered camera, added UI/text, extra rays and guides, and less faithful composition.
